 singapore Woman reports snake, upset by NParks' response
 The snake was eventually captured by a snake handler and safely placed in a plastic container. PHOTO: Facebook/Vivien Goh PUBLISHED ON November 02, 2026 7:03 AM BY Asyiqin Nadzri A woman has expressed frustration with the response she received from the National Parks Board (NParks) after reporting a snake spotted outside her neighbour's home.
 In a Facebook post shared on Sunday (Nov 1), Vivien Goh recounted calling NParks after encountering the snake at her apartment lobby.
 She said the staff member who answered the hotline repeatedly asked her to take a photograph of the animal and send it over WhatsApp.
 However, Goh said she did not have WhatsApp on the phone she was carrying at the time.
 "There is something very wrong with the person manning the NParks hotline today," she wrote.
 She added that she had explained her situation but was still asked to send the photograph four times.
 "I can't go back in because there is a snake at my apartment lobby, can you please just send someone over!" she recounted telling the staff member.
 Goh later shared photographs of the snake, which she said she had taken from behind a glass door while it was on the steps outside her neighbour's home.
 She added in the comments that she had earlier jumped over the snake, which moved "really fast".
 [[nid:749452]]
 Goh questions how the snake would be monitored
 In an update in the comments, Goh claimed that she called NParks again and was told that the animal would be monitored.
 She questioned how this would be done if nobody was physically present to remove the snake.
 "So the update is, when I called in again, is that they will 'monitor' it. How are they monitoring it when no one is here to take the snake away?!" she wrote.
 The incident prompted some commenters to suggest that she contact the Animal Concerns Research and Education Society (ACRES), which also operates a wildlife rescue hotline.
 Others felt that the snake should be left alone to slither away, particularly if it was small and not posing an immediate threat.
 One commenter suggested that NParks and ACRES also had to consider the safety of the animal, adding that members of the public could consider contacting a pest controller depending on the situation.
 Another commenter offered a more sympathetic view of NParks' request for photographs, suggesting that the agency could have wanted to verify the sighting before dispatching someone.
 Snake eventually caught by handler
 Goh subsequently shared a second update, expressing relief after a snake handler arrived and picked up the animal.
 She described watching as the handler calmly picked up the snake and placed it gently into a plastic container.
 Goh said she was initially surprised by how small the snake appeared, as she had estimated it to be about 1.2m long when she first spotted it.
 The handler reportedly told her that she might have overestimated its size because she had zoomed in on the photograph.
 AsiaOne has contacted Vivien Goh and NParks for more information.
